article.headline: Why AI Data Center Power Forecasts Keep Missing the Mark
article.lede: Somewhere between the spreadsheet and the substation, the math breaks. Analysts and investors projecting 20, 30, even 50 gigawatts of new AI data center capacity per year by 2030 are, according to infrastructure observers like Shanu Mathew, confusing a growth rate with a physical possibility. The constraints, he argues, are not easing — they are compounding.
article.body:
The surge in AI compute demand set off a race to build. Hyperscalers announced eye-watering capital expenditure plans — hundreds of billions of dollars committed to new campuses — and a cohort of investors extrapolated forward, modeling data center power additions as though they were semiconductor fabs scaling with Moore's Law. The result was a genre of forecast: 20 GW added in 2026, 30 in 2027, 50 by 2029. Impressive curves on a slide; less convincing once you trace them to the physical world.

The bottlenecks are structural and slow to clear. *Interconnection queues* — the backlog of projects waiting for permission to connect to the electrical grid — have swollen to the point where wait times in major US markets routinely exceed five years. Transformer lead times, which ran roughly 12 months before the AI boom, stretched past three years for large units as orders piled up and manufacturing capacity failed to keep pace. Permitting for new transmission lines moves on geological time in most jurisdictions. Each of these constraints is independent; all of them must be resolved before a single server rack draws power.

Mathew's frustration is epistemological as much as technical. **Spreadsheet extrapolation** takes a trend — data center power demand doubling, say, every two years — and assumes the growth rate propagates indefinitely. Constraint-aware modeling asks a different question: given finite transformer factories, finite grid capacity, finite permitting staff, what is the realistic throughput? The two approaches can produce wildly different numbers, and in conversations with tech investors Mathew reports being told, repeatedly, that he simply did not understand the pace of change.

The stakes are not merely academic. Overestimating build rates by a factor of two or three has downstream consequences: utilities that over-invest in generation anticipating load that arrives late, equipment manufacturers that expand capacity only to face a demand air pocket, and AI companies whose roadmaps assume compute availability that the grid cannot deliver on schedule. The irony is that the people most confident in the 50 GW/year scenario are often the furthest removed from the transformer yards and grid operators who would have to execute it.

concepts.definition: The formal backlog of power generation and large-load projects awaiting permission to connect to the electrical grid. Grid operators process requests sequentially, study their impact on reliability, and approve connections in order. When demand surges — as it has with AI data centers — the queue lengthens and wait times stretch from months to years.

A forecasting approach that takes a recent trend and projects it forward at the same rate, without modeling the physical, logistical, or regulatory limits that slow growth as scale increases. It tends to be accurate over short horizons and dangerously optimistic over long ones when the system is approaching saturation or a scarce resource.

The time between ordering a large electrical transformer and taking delivery. Transformers are bespoke, heavy industrial equipment manufactured by a small number of facilities worldwide. As AI data center orders surged, lead times for high-voltage units extended dramatically, becoming one of the binding constraints on how fast new capacity can actually come online.

A measure of electrical power capacity. One gigawatt can power roughly 750,000 average US homes. In the AI infrastructure context, analysts use GW to describe how much grid power a portfolio of data centers is contracted to consume. Estimates for total AI-driven new load additions in the US through 2030 have ranged from under 50 GW to over 100 GW, depending on assumptions.
